newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico parties fail to agree on election funding.
newsitem.headline: Mexico parties fail to agree on election funding.

text.p: Mexico's main political parties failed on Wednesday to thrash out an agreement on election campaign financing and the matter will now be sent to Congress for a decision, a government official said.

President Ernesto Zedillo will send an electoral reform bill to Congress shortly which will "contain all the accords reached by the political parties, which are the immense majority, as well as detailing the points where agreement has not been complete," deputy Interior Minister Arturo Nunez Jimenez said.

The government is pressing ahead without complete agreement among the parties because of the need to establish clear electoral rules before mid-term legislative elections due on July 6 next year, Nunez told reporters.
"The electoral timetable imposes the immediate need to have a regulatory framework that will give certainty and finality to the electoral process," Nunez said.

The decision followed days of meetings on campaign financing between Interior Minister Emilio Chuayffet and leaders of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party and the opposition National Action, Democratic Revolution and Labour parties.

The PRI, in power since 1929, had proposed the government should give political parties a total of $227 million for the 1997 vote, a sum opposition parties called absurdly high when the country is barely emerging from a deep economic crisis following the December 1994 peso crash.

The sum is almost as much as the total of $277.4 million President Bill Clinton and challenger Bob Dole were allowed to spend between them by the Federal Election Commission in their presidential battle.
In the 1997 elections, halfway through the six-year term of Zedillo, Mexicans will choose a new Chamber of Deputies and renew a quarter of the Senate.
The reform package aims to eliminate, among other things, allegations of corrupt practices that critics say have helped the PRI to stay in power continuously for the last 67 years.
